sections.h2: What does the Texas homestead exemption do for a homeowner?
sections.html:
It removes part of your home's appraised value from the base that local taxing units tax, so the bill shrinks even though the market value does not change. Appraisal districts set value as of January 1, so your status on that date drives the year's bill. The Texas Comptroller lays out three layers: a mandatory school district exemption, optional local exemptions, and extra relief for older or disabled owners.

Texas has no state property tax. Each taxing unit applies the exemption to its own levy, so two neighbors served by different units can see different savings.

sections.h2: How much is the general residence homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) sets a $140,000 school district exemption on a residence homestead. Under Sec. 11.13(n) any other unit may choose a percentage exemption, capped at 20 percent of value, with a $5,000 minimum.

  • School districts: $140,000, mandatory.
  • Cities, counties and others: optional, at the unit's discretion.
  • Counties with farm-to-market or flood control levies: $3,000 (Sec. 11.13(a)).

Ask your appraisal district which units serving your address have adopted a local option, because the Comptroller describes it as a choice each unit makes.

sections.h2: Who qualifies as the owner of a homestead?
sections.html:
Two tests apply: you own an interest in the house, and it is where you mainly live. A second claimed homestead, in Texas or elsewhere, disqualifies you.

A mid-year purchase still earns the exemption for the remaining months if the seller was not already getting it. Heirs absent from the recorded deed show the appraisal district an ownership affidavit, the prior owner's death certificate, a utility bill and any court record citation.

sections.h2: What extra relief exists at age 65 or with a disability?
sections.html:
Age 65 or disability adds $60,000 at the school district level (Sec. 11.13(c)). Local units may match with their own under Sec. 11.13(d), starting at $3,000.

Disability is judged by the Social Security benefit definition. In some cases a widow or widower aged 55 or more keeps the late spouse's over-65 benefit.

These owners also receive a freeze on school tax. Sec. 11.26 bars the district from raising their total yearly bill on the homestead, using the tax of the first year they qualified as the base. The freeze can follow the owner to a new Texas homestead, in proportion, and can continue for a surviving spouse aged 55 or older. Added improvements beyond ordinary repairs can lift it. Sec. 11.261 allows counties, cities and junior college districts to adopt their own.

sections.h2: How does the 10 percent appraisal cap work?
sections.html:
Once you qualify, appraised value on the homestead may climb at most 10 percent a year, new improvements aside. Sec. 23.23 takes the lesser of market value or last year's appraised value plus 10 percent plus improvements.

It starts the January 1 after your first qualifying year. A higher rate from a taxing unit can still raise the bill, since the cap governs value only.

Disabled veterans get an exemption on any one property they own, scaled to their VA disability rating. The Comptroller prints these amounts under Sec. 11.22.

A veteran aged 65 or older with a rating of at least 10 percent, a veteran who is totally blind in one or both eyes, or one who lost use of a limb may receive $12,000. An unmarried surviving spouse and children under 18 may qualify too.

At a 100 percent rating, or 100 percent unemployability, the whole residence homestead is exempt under Sec. 11.131, and an unmarried surviving spouse may keep it on stated conditions. A charity-donated homestead falls under Sec. 11.132, where the exempt share follows the rating. Sec. 11.133 fully exempts the home of a surviving spouse of a service member killed in the line of duty.

sections.h2: How do the layers combine for different owners?
sections.html:
Think of the exemption as a stack that grows with your circumstances. Each layer applies only to the taxing units that grant it.

  • Any residence homestead owner: the mandatory $140,000 school district exemption.
  • Owner aged 65 or older, or disabled: that same $140,000 plus $60,000, along with the school tax freeze.
  • Disabled veteran: a separate exemption on one property, scaled from $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, or total at a 100 percent rating on the residence homestead.
  • Any owner in a unit with a local option: a percentage exemption of up to 20 percent of value on top.

The Comptroller's pages describe each as a distinct provision, so an owner who fits two groups should ask the appraisal district how the two apply together on the actual bill.

sections.h2: What should an applicant bring to the appraisal district?
sections.html:
Bring proof of ownership and proof that the house is your main home. The district decides what it accepts, so check its website or call before you go.

  • The deed, or for an heir the ownership affidavit and death certificate.
  • A current utility bill showing the property address.
  • For age-based relief, proof of age; for disability relief, proof of Social Security disability benefits.
  • For veterans, VA documentation of the disability rating.

Applying for a veteran exemption does not require waiting for the next spring cycle in every case, because Sec. 11.22 allows late applications for up to five years after the delinquency date.

sections.h2: When and where do you apply?
sections.html:
The county appraisal district takes the application; the school district and Comptroller do not. For the general homestead exemption the filing must come before May 1, and April 30 also closes some other exemption and special-appraisal applications.

  • Homestead exemptions use Form 50-114.
  • The disabled veteran exemption under Sec. 11.22 uses Form 50-135.
  • Veterans under Sec. 11.22 get up to five years past the delinquency date to apply, and the surviving spouse of a veteran with a donated homestead gets two.

Value notices for single-family homesteads start around April 1. Disputing the number is a separate step from the exemption and has its own cutoff, usually May 15 unless 30 days after delivery falls later.

sections.h2: How does the exemption matter when you sell?
sections.html:
Your exemption leaves with your ownership, but that year's lien stays on the land. It attaches January 1 for taxes, penalties and interest, so unpaid amounts normally get cleared at closing.

Whoever owned on January 1 is liable for the year's bill and can be sued after selling. Delinquency starts February 1 for bills mailed in October, with penalty and interest added.

For a sale involving back taxes, unrecorded heirs or a house you have moved out of, get a payoff from the tax office and your exemption status from the district first.

faqs.q: Is the Texas homestead exemption automatic?
faqs.a: No, you must apply with Form 50-114 at the appraisal district, in general before May 1.

faqs.q: Can I get both the $140,000 and the $60,000 school exemptions?
faqs.a: Yes, for owners aged 65 or older or disabled, the two stack: $140,000 under Sec. 11.13(b) plus $60,000 under Sec. 11.13(c).

faqs.q: Does the 10 percent cap lower my tax rate?
faqs.a: No. It slows growth in appraised value only. Each unit sets its rate separately, and new improvements come on top of the capped value.

faqs.q: Can a surviving spouse keep the over-65 exemption?
faqs.a: In some cases, if the spouse is 55 or older; the school tax ceiling may continue too. The appraisal district can confirm your situation.

faqs.q: What if I inherited a house and am not on the deed?
faqs.a: Bring four items to the district: an ownership affidavit, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation.
